title: Ganesha, the scribe
hook: Ganesha writes down the Mahabharata without a pause, and why Hindus treat every letter as holy
carry: akshara: the letter that does not perish
tomorrow: why would a great teacher fold his hands to a man he'd just told to move?

segments.voice: Yesterday, little Prahlada told his father what he'd really learned at school: hearing, singing, remembering, the first ways to love God. Today, the last day of the sounds, and the god who wrote the holiest words down.

The sage Vyasa has the whole Mahabharata in his head, the longest poem anyone knows, and he needs someone to write it down. As the story is told, he asks Ganesha. Ganesha agrees, on one condition: once you start, you never pause. Vyasa agrees, and adds his own: then you never write a verse until you understand it. So they begin. Whenever Vyasa needs a breath, he drops in a knotty verse, and Ganesha has to stop and think. And in a telling families love, the pen breaks in the middle of a line. Ganesha doesn't stop. He snaps off one of his own tusks, and keeps writing.
screen: `NEVER PAUSE.` → `NEVER WRITE WHAT YOU DON'T UNDERSTAND.` → `THE PEN BREAKS.` → `HE BREAKS HIS TUSK.`

segments.voice: That's one reason pictures of Ganesha show him holding a broken tusk. Why would a god give up part of himself for letters? Because in Sanskrit a letter is an akshara, and akshara also means imperishable: what does not wear away. The Bhagavad Gita calls Om the one-syllable Brahman, the whole of reality in one sound. So in Hindu thought, sounds and letters aren't just tools. They're holy. Even their order means something: the old study of sounds lines the letters up as a walk through the mouth, ka at the throat, cha at the palate, the curled-back ta at the roof of the mouth, the plain ta at the teeth, pa at the lips, so every letter has its own place. You can see the teaching in ordinary homes. In many Hindu families, if your foot touches a book, you touch it to your forehead, a small apology to learning. At Saraswati Puja, books and pens rest at the goddess's feet for the day. And in Kerala, on Vijayadashami, a small child sits in an elder's lap and traces first letters in a plate of rice, a rite called Vidyarambham. The first words traced are often a bow to Ganesha. Learning starts with the one who broke his tusk to keep the words going.
screen: `THE BROKEN TUSK.` · `AKSHARA: IMPERISHABLE. OM: BRAHMAN.` · `EACH LETTER HAS ITS PLACE.` · `A BOOK TOUCHED TO THE FOREHEAD.` · then, large: `THE LETTER THAT DOES NOT PERISH.`

segments.voice: Before you write anything today, a note, a message, a page, do what many Hindu families do at the top of a new account book: write Om, or Shri, first. If you don't pray, take one slow breath before the first word instead. Then sit for a minute with the hands resting, and let the breath rise from the chest and leave at the lips, the way the letters do.
The sounds: lined up from the throat to the lips, each one an akshara, a letter that does not perish.
Something to keep: akshara, the letter that does not perish. Ganesha broke his tusk to keep the words going. Last day of the sounds.

Vyasa.meaning: the sage who composed the Mahabharata

akshara.meaning: a letter or syllable; also, imperishable

Saraswati.meaning: the goddess of learning, music and speech

Vidyarambham.meaning: the start of learning: a child's first letters, traced in rice

Devanagari.meaning: the script Sanskrit is usually written in
